question: What is grace, and can anyone do good without it?
short: Can we do good without grace?

answers.label: No: grace must go first, even to begin to believe
Yes: our nature, God's gift, can keep his commands

overview.text: Pelagius, about 416, taught that a person can be without sin and keep God's commands easily, if he wishes. For him grace meant our God-given nature, the law, and Christ's teaching and example.

Augustine's prayer "Give what you command, and command what you will" sums up the opposite view: every good will is God's gift. The Council of Orange (529) made that the Western rule, and Trent repeated it.

quotes.author: Pelagius (quoted by Augustine)
quotes.work: Letter, quoted in Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius
quotes.english: By the judgment of fourteen bishops our definition was approved, in which we said that a person can be without sin and easily keep God's commandments, if he wishes.
quotes.original: quattuordecim episcoporum sententia definitio nostra comprobata est, qua diximus posse hominem sine peccato esse et dei mandata facile custodire, si uelit.
quotes.context: Pelagius wrote this after a synod at Diospolis in Palestine (415) cleared him. Augustine's reply: "if he wishes" leaves out God's help. Pelagius said grace is given in our nature and in the law and teaching.

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: All my hope is nowhere but in your great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will. You command us to be continent. ... And as I knew, someone says, that no one can be continent unless God gives it, this too was wisdom, to know whose gift it is.
quotes.original: Et tota spes mea non nisi in magna misericordia tua. da quod iubes et iube quod uis. imperas nobis continentiam. et cum scirem, ait quidam, quia nemo potest esse continens nisi deus det, et hoc ipsum erat sapientiae, scire cuius esset hoc donum.
quotes.context: "Give what you command": the prayer Pelagius could not bear to hear read at Rome, as Augustine later recalled (On the Gift of Perseverance 20.53). The quotation inside is Wisdom 8:21.

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: For we do not deny that human nature can be without sin, nor should we in any way deny that it can be perfected, since we do not deny that it can make progress; but we say that this comes about by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, with his help, so that it may be righteous and blessed, by the one who created it to be.
quotes.original: Non enim abnuimus humanam naturam posse esse sine peccato, aut ullo modo negare debemus perfici posse, quam proficere non negamus, sed gratia Dei per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum: eo adjuvante fieri dicimus, ut iusta et beata sit, a quo creata est ut sit.
quotes.context: Augustine answers Pelagius's book On Nature: sinlessness itself is not denied. What is denied is that our nature can reach it without grace.

source.edition: Migne PL 44 (1845), De natura et gratia 68

quotes.author: Council of Carthage
quotes.english: It was also resolved: whoever says that the grace of justification is given us so that what we are commanded to do by free choice we may more easily fulfil through grace, as if, even if grace were not given, we could, not easily indeed, but still could, fulfil the divine commandments without it, let him be anathema. For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, 'Without me you can do things with difficulty', but said, 'Without me you can do nothing' (John 15:5).
quotes.original: Item placuit, ut quicunque dixerit, ideo nobis gratiam iustificationis dari, ut, quod facere per liberum iubemur arbitrium, facilius possimus implere per gratiam, tamquam et si gratia non daretur, non quidem facile, sed tamen possimus etiam sine illa implere divina mandata, A. S. ... De fructibus enim mandatorum Dominus loquebatur, ubi non ait: Sine me difficilius potestis facere, sed ait: Sine me nihil potestis facere.
quotes.context: The African bishops at Carthage (418) condemned Pelagius's teaching canon by canon; Pope Zosimus approved the canons, and they became the West's rule on grace before Orange.

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: In them I said to our God, and I said it often: 'Give what you command, and command what you will.' ... What, then, does God command first and most of all, if not that we believe in him? So this too he himself gives, if it was rightly said to him, 'Give what you command.'
quotes.original: in eis certe dixi Deo nostro, et saepe dixi: Da quod iubes, et iube quod vis... Quid vero primitus et maxime Deus iubet, nisi ut credamus in eum? Et hoc ergo ipse dat, si bene illi dictum est, Da quod iubes.
quotes.context: Augustine, near the end of his life, recalls that Pelagius at Rome could not bear to hear the prayer from his Confessions quoted. Even faith, the first thing God commands, is God's gift.

quotes.author: Council of Orange
quotes.english: If anyone says that mercy is given by God to us when, without God's grace, we believe, will, desire, try, labor, keep watch, study, ask, seek and knock, but does not confess that it is by the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit in us that we believe, will, or are able to do all these things as we ought ... he resists the apostle (1 Corinthians 4:7; 15:10).
quotes.original: Si quis sine gratia Dei credentibus, volentibus, desiderantibus, conantibus, laborantibus, vigilantibus, studentibus, petentibus, quaerentibus, pulsantibus nobis misericordiam dicit conferri divinitus, non autem ut credamus, velimus, vel haec omnia, sicut oportet, agere valeamus, per infusionem et inspirationem Sancti Spiritus in nobis fieri confitetur ... resistit Apostolo dicenti
quotes.context: A small Gallic council, later approved by Pope Boniface II (531). It settled the West against the view that the first step toward God is ours.

quotes.author: Council of Trent
quotes.english: If anyone says that without the prevenient inspiration of the Holy Spirit and his help a person can believe, hope, love or repent as he ought, so that the grace of justification may be given to him: let him be anathema.
quotes.original: Si quis dixerit, sine praeveniente Spiritus Sancti inspiratione atque eius adiutorio hominem credere, sperare, diligere aut poenitere posse, sicut oportet, ut ei iustificationis gratia conferatur: A. S.
quotes.context: On this point Trent and the Reformers agreed: no one turns to God without grace going first.

gaps.author: John Cassian
gaps.why: The view that the first stirrings of good will can be ours. Orange answers it.

gaps.author: Pelagius
gaps.why: Pelagius on human nature in his own words.

method: Every early quote was read in its Greek or Latin and translated for this page by Claude (Opus 5.5) on 13 October 2026. Each line names the printed edition it was read from.
